input.question: How can splitting atoms (fission) and joining atoms (fusion) BOTH release huge amounts of energy?
input.ground_truth: If you fuse two Hydrogen atoms to produce a Helium atom, the Helium atom will weigh slightly less than two Hydrogen atoms. The missing mass became energy during fusion. The "daughter products" of a fission reaction will also weigh less than the original atoms; again, the lost mass became energy. There would be no point in putting a fusion reactor next to a fission reactor; in both cases, "Energy equals Mass multiplied by the square of the speed of light" is incredibly generous. It's not like we're running out of *mass*, after all.

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine you have a big, squishy ball of playdough. If you break it into two smaller pieces (that's like **splitting atoms**, or **fission**), you notice that the pieces don’t stick together as tightly as before. When you break the ball apart, a little bit of “stuff” (called energy) flies out. That’s energy!

Now, imagine you have two tiny pieces of playdough. If you push them together really, really hard and stick them into one big ball (that's like **joining atoms**, or **fusion**), you also have to use a lot of force. But when they finally stick together, some of that force turns into energy and pops out, just like when you broke the big ball apart!

So, whether you break a big ball into two smaller ones or squish two small ones into one big one, you get a lot of energy out! That’s why both splitting atoms and joining atoms can give us a HUGE burst of energy!
